indicators.title: Indicators
indicators.description: The four open series behind the estimate: weather-corrected electricity, business climate, insolvency openings and the France–Germany yield spread.
indicators.intro: Each series updates automatically from its source. Values are monthly.
ind.electricity.note: National consumption, corrected for temperature, day of the week and month. It is the signal most closely tied to month-to-month production.

ind.insolvencies.note: Safeguard, receivership and liquidation proceedings opened, from BODACC notices.
ind.spread.note: The gap between French and German 10-year government bond yields: a measure of perceived risk on France.

model.title: The model, formula by formula
model.description: The exact formulas behind the estimate, today’s coefficients and the full calculation for the latest month, with the code that produces them.
model.intro: Every number on this site comes from the formulas below. The coefficients are re-estimated every day; the ones shown here belong to the model that produced the estimate of {date}, trained on {n} months ({from} to {to}, excluding March to July 2020).
model.s1.text: The monthly change in the industrial production index (IPI, total industry, seasonally and working-day adjusted), in percent, computed as a log difference:
model.s2.text: Electricity use depends first of all on temperature. A regression on {days} days of history isolates that effect. For each day d, the log of mean consumption is explained by heating need, cooling need, the day of the week w(d) and the month of the year m(d):
model.s2.dd: where T is the day’s mean temperature, weighted by the population of 8 large cities:
model.s2.fit: Estimated coefficients: consumption rises {hdd} per degree below 15 °C and {cdd} per degree above 20 °C. What remains, the residual, measures activity. It is averaged over the month, then compared with the month before:
model.s3.text: Each input is used only from its actual publication date. The estimate for month t is made at the start of month t+1.
model.s4.text: Each input is first standardised, so the weights are comparable:
model.s4.pred: The estimate is a weighted sum:
model.s4.loss: The weights minimise the squared error over the training months, plus a penalty that pulls them towards zero and limits overfitting:
model.s4.alpha: The penalty α is chosen among {count} values from {lo} to {hi} by leave-one-out cross-validation. Chosen value: α = {alpha}. The constant b₀ is {b0}: the average monthly growth over the training months.
model.s5.text: Here is the estimate rebuilt input by input. The constant plus the contributions gives exactly the published figure; the program checks this at every update.
model.chart_desc: Contribution of each input, in percentage points. Right means up.
model.s6.text: The 80% range comes from past errors: 80% of the test errors, excluding the pandemic, were smaller than q₈₀ = {q} points.
model.s6.level: For the index level two months after the last release, the range is widened by a factor of √2, assuming monthly errors are independent.
model.s7.text: The naive forecast carries forward the latest published growth. Its coefficients today:
model.s7.eval: Both methods are compared by root mean squared error and the Diebold–Mariano test, which checks whether the accuracy gap is larger than chance:
model.s8.text: Excerpts of the Python code that runs every day, read straight from the repository when the site is built.
model.code.training: Which months are used for training (step 3)
goals.title: What this site does
goals.anticipate.text: Estimate French industrial production about six weeks before INSEE publishes it, from data that comes out every day.
goals.uncertainty.text: Publish every estimate with its range and the full record of its past errors, misses included.
goals.transparency.text: Data, formulas, coefficients and code are public, so every number can be checked and reproduced.
goals.open_data.text: Bring scattered French and European open data together, readable in French and English.
diag.title: Model diagnostics
diag.intro: Beyond the average error, these checks test whether the estimate is well calibrated, stable over time and unbiased. All use the test’s months excluding the pandemic.
diag.table_caption: Every model, every indicator (excluding March to July 2020)
diag.table_note: Bias: average of estimate minus published figure; negative means the estimate runs slightly low on average. R²: the share of the naive forecast’s error the model removes. Gradient boosting does worse than ridge, so it isn’t published.
diag.coverage: Over {n} months since {from}, the published figure fell inside the 80% range in {share} of months. Each range used only the errors known on its date: a well-calibrated range aims for 80%.
diag.scatter_desc: Each dot is a month, excluding the pandemic. On the diagonal the estimate would be perfect. A cloud flatter than the diagonal means a cautious estimate that moves less than reality.
diag.rolling_desc: Root mean squared error over the previous 24 months, in points: lower is better.
diag.recent_better: Over the latest 24 months, the estimate beats the naive forecast ({rmse} against {rmse_ar}).
diag.recent_worse: Over the latest 24 months, the estimate does slightly worse than the naive forecast ({rmse} against {rmse_ar}): the gain measured over the whole period hasn’t held up recently.
diag.hist_desc: Estimate minus published figure, in points, in 0.5-point bins. Mean bias: {bias}.
diag.weights_desc: Weight of each standardised input at every monthly refit since {from}. Flat lines mean a stable model; a weight that changes sign deserves attention.

rss.title: France Economic Pulse: estimates
model.s9: 8. Why this model: the variants tested
model.s9.text: Two improvements to the weather correction were tested with exactly the same protocol as the published model: every month since 2016, retrained only on the data available at that date.
model.s9.recent: Recent seasons: each year’s seasonal pattern is estimated from the three years up to it, instead of the whole history. It follows changes in habits better, such as those after the energy crisis.
model.s9.holidays: Public holidays: an input flags the eleven French public holidays, when consumption drops as on a Sunday.
model.s9.caption: Variants compared, excluding the pandemic (recomputed every day)
model.s9.naive_note: For comparison, the naive forecast’s error over the last 24 months is {ar}.
model.s9.tradeoff: Recent seasons remove the September bias and do better over the last two years. But over the whole period they make larger errors and get the direction right less often: estimating each year from only three years makes the seasonal pattern less stable. Public holidays change almost nothing.
model.s9.rule: A variant replaces the published model only if it does better over the whole test period. Picking a variant because it shines over the latest months would be choosing with hindsight: 24 months are too few to tell real progress from chance. So the published model stays, and its September bias is flagged on the Method page.
model.s9.keep: Today, the published model is still the most accurate over the whole period.
model.s9.switch: Today, the “{variant}” variant does better over the whole period: adopting it will be reconsidered.
model.s9.revisit: This comparison is recomputed at every update. It will be reviewed when the real-time track record covers twelve months, or sooner if a variant takes the lead over the whole period.

gdp.title: Quarterly GDP: an experimental model
gdp.description: An attempt to estimate French GDP before INSEE, from industrial production, surveys and consumption. It doesn’t beat a naive forecast by a significant margin: published for transparency.
gdp.warning: Experimental. None of these models forecasts GDP significantly better than a naive forecast (last quarter’s growth). They are published to show the work and its limits, not as a reliable estimate.
gdp.lede: For {quarter}, the models range from {lo} to {hi}. INSEE’s first figure is expected around {date}.
gdp.table_caption: Estimates for {quarter} and each model’s past accuracy
gdp.table_note: Past error: test from {from} to {to}, {n} quarters excluding 2020–2021, using only what was known on the day of INSEE’s first figure. p: the probability that the gap with the naive forecast is due to chance.
gdp.chart_title: GDP growth: published figures and past estimates
gdp.chart_desc: Quarterly change in real GDP (%), since 2016, excluding 2020–2021. Each estimate uses only the data available on its date.
gdp.how: A bridge equation links quarterly GDP growth to industrial production growth. Months INSEE hasn’t published yet are filled with this site’s monthly estimate. Two variants add the services business climate and household consumption of goods. All were tested as on the day of INSEE’s first estimate, about 30 days after the quarter ends.
gdp.why: Since 2016, French quarterly GDP growth has been small and steady: last quarter’s growth already captures most of it. Industrial production really helps when all three months of the quarter are known, but the third is published after GDP, and estimating it erases the gain. Surveys add little at this horizon.
gdp.next: A better monthly estimate of production, or real-time consumption data such as the card payments the Banque de France uses, which aren’t openly available. The test reruns every day: if a model takes the lead, this page will say so.
